title: Career Launch
tagline: Land the job, nail the interview, get paid what you're worth.
description: Go from no experience to a job offer: find openings, write a resume that shows results, and answer interview questions with clear stories. Then learn the habits that get you trusted at work, how to negotiate pay, how side income is taxed, and how to compare college, trades and certificates by what they really return.

units.title: Finding Work
units.description: Where jobs come from, resumes that show results, and applications that get noticed.

levels.title: Where Jobs Come From
levels.summary: Networking, job boards, applying directly and spotting fake job offers.

steps.title: The hidden job market
steps.body:
Many jobs are filled through people who already know someone: a referral, a past manager, a friend of a friend. A recommendation from a trusted employee gets your application read.

Good places to look:
- **People you know**: family, friends' parents, teachers, coaches, past bosses
- **Company career pages** for businesses you'd like to work for
- **Job boards** and your school's career center
- **Walking in** for local jobs: restaurants, shops, trades

> Networking just means letting people know what you're looking for and being someone they'd recommend.

steps.prompt: You want a summer job at a local landscaping company. Your neighbor's cousin works there. What's the best first move?

options.text: Ask your neighbor to introduce you, then message the cousin briefly: who you are, what you want, and whether they'd pass along your name.
options.feedback: Great. A short, specific, polite ask makes it easy for people to help.

options.text: Only apply online so you don't bother anyone.
options.feedback: Applying is fine, but skipping a warm connection wastes your best advantage.

options.text: Ask the cousin to get you hired, today.
options.feedback: Too much pressure. Ask for an introduction or advice, not a guaranteed job.

steps.explain: Warm introductions turn you from a random name into someone a current employee vouches for. Always thank people who help.

steps.title: Searching smart
steps.body:
Applying to 100 random jobs usually works worse than 15 targeted ones.

- Read the posting. Note **required** vs **preferred** skills. If you meet most requirements, apply.
- Use specific search terms: "entry level", "no experience", "trainee", "apprentice".
- Track applications in a simple sheet: company, role, date applied, contact, follow-up date.
- Research pay for the role before you apply. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Outlook Handbook lists typical pay and what training each job needs.

steps.prompt: A posting lists 6 required skills. You have 5 of them, plus related experience. What should you do?
options: Don't apply: you need 100% of the requirements
Apply, and show the strongest matches clearly in your resume
Apply and claim you have all 6
Wait a year until you have the last one
steps.explain: Postings are wish lists. If you meet most requirements, apply and make your matching skills easy to see. Never lie: it can get an offer withdrawn or get you fired later.

steps.title: Fake job offers
steps.body:
Job scams target people who are eager to start. Warning signs:
- They ask **you** to pay for training, equipment or a starter kit.
- They send a **check** and ask you to send part of it to someone else.
- The job is **reshipping packages**.
- They promise big money for little work, or hire you after a chat-only "interview".
- They want your SSN or bank info before any real offer.

Real employers pay you, not the other way around. Look the company up yourself and contact it through its official site.

steps.prompt: Which are red flags for a job scam? Select all that apply.
options: You must buy a $199 starter kit before your first shift
The interview happens only over a messaging app, and you're hired in 20 minutes
The company asks for references after an in-person interview
They mail you a check and ask you to send part of it to a vendor
You fill out a W-4 and I-9 on your first day
steps.explain: Paying to work, instant hiring by chat, and check-forwarding are classic scams. References and W-4/I-9 forms on day one are normal parts of real hiring.

steps.prompt: Put a focused job search routine in order.
items: Decide on 1-3 types of roles you want
Tell people you know what you're looking for
Find postings and research each company
Tailor your resume to each posting and apply
Log the application and follow up after about a week
steps.explain: Clear targets make networking and tailoring possible. Tracking and follow-up separate you from people who apply and forget.

steps.prompt: A real employer will sometimes ask you to pay for your own background check or training before you're hired.
steps.explain: Legitimate employers don't charge applicants to get a job. Paying upfront for the promise of work is a top sign of a scam.

steps.prompt: List five people who might know about jobs in a field you're interested in, and one sentence you could send each of them.
steps.placeholder: 1) ___ 2) ___ ... Message: 'Hi ___, I'm looking for ___. Do you know anyone I could talk to?'

levels.title: Resumes That Show Results
levels.summary: Action + result + number bullets, a clean layout and tailoring for each job.

steps.title: What a resume is for
steps.body:
A hiring manager often skims a resume in seconds. Its only job is to get you an interview.

A simple, one-page resume for an early-career job:
- **Header**: name, phone, professional email, city/state
- **Experience**: jobs, volunteering, school projects, sports leadership, babysitting, mowing lawns all count
- **Education**
- **Skills**: tools, software, languages, certifications

Use a plain layout with clear headings. Fancy graphics and tables can confuse the software many companies use to scan applications.

steps.title: The bullet formula: action + result + number
steps.body:
Weak bullets list duties. Strong bullets show impact.

> **Action verb + what you did + result, with a number when you can**

- Weak: "Responsible for helping customers."
- Strong: "Helped 60+ customers a shift find products, earning a 4.8/5 store survey rating."

- Weak: "Did social media for club."
- Strong: "Grew the robotics club's Instagram from 120 to 450 followers in one semester."

Numbers can be counts, money, time saved, percentages or ratings.

steps.prompt: Which resume bullet is strongest?
options: Worked at the register
Responsible for cash handling duties
Handled $3,000+ in daily cash sales with zero drawer errors over 8 months
Hard worker who is good with money
steps.explain: It starts with an action, shows scale ($3,000+ daily) and a result (zero errors over 8 months). Self-descriptions like 'hard worker' are claims, not proof.

steps.prompt: Rebuild this bullet in the formula's order: action verb, what you did, result with a number.
items: Organized
a canned-food drive across 4 homerooms
collecting 1,200 items for the local food bank
steps.explain: 'Organized a canned-food drive across 4 homerooms, collecting 1,200 items for the local food bank.' Verb first, then the work, then the measurable result.

steps.prompt: Match each weak phrase to a stronger action verb.
steps.explain: Strong, specific verbs make you the person who acted, not someone who was around while things happened.

steps.title: Tailor it every time
steps.body:
Keep a long **master resume** with everything. For each application, make a copy and:
- Move the most relevant experience to the top.
- Use the **same words** the posting uses for skills (if they say "customer service", don't only say "client support").
- Cut bullets that don't help for this job.

Then proofread: one typo can sink an application. Read it out loud, and ask someone else to check it.

Save and send as a PDF named like **FirstName-LastName-Resume.pdf**.

steps.prompt: Which belong on a resume for an entry-level job? Select all that apply.
options: Volunteer work with results
Your Social Security number
Certifications like CPR or a forklift license
A professional email address
An email like partyking2009@...
steps.explain: Volunteering, certifications and a professional email help. Never put your SSN on a resume, and use a simple firstname.lastname style email.

steps.prompt: If you've never had a paid job, you have nothing to put under Experience.
steps.explain: Volunteering, school projects, team captain roles, family business help, babysitting and lawn mowing all show responsibility. Label the section 'Experience', not 'Work History'.

steps.prompt: Write two resume bullets for something you've done (a job, team, club, project or chore business) using action + result + number.

levels.title: Cover Letters and Applications
levels.summary: A short cover letter that connects you to the job, and polished applications.

steps.title: A cover letter in three short paragraphs
steps.body:
Not every job asks for one, but when it's optional, a good one can help.

1. **Hook**: the job you're applying for and one sentence on why this company specifically.
2. **Proof**: 1-2 examples that match what they need, with results.
3. **Close**: thank them and say you'd welcome an interview.

Keep it under one page, ideally under 250 words. Address a real person if you can find the name. Never send the same generic letter everywhere.

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a cover letter in order.
items: Greeting to the hiring manager by name
The role you're applying for and why this company
One or two examples of matching results
Thanks and a request for an interview
Sign-off with your name and contact info
steps.explain: Open with fit, prove it with examples, close with a clear next step.

steps.prompt: Which opening line is strongest for a cover letter to a bike shop?
options: To whom it may concern, I am applying for any open position.
I'm applying for the Bike Mechanic Trainee role because I've repaired and resold 15 bikes this year and love your shop's community rides.
I really need a job and you're close to my house.
My name is Jordan and I am 17 years old.
steps.explain: It names the role, gives a concrete, relevant result, and shows you know the shop. The others are generic or about what you need instead of what you offer.

steps.title: Applications: details matter
steps.body:
- Fill out **every field**. "See resume" looks lazy.
- Have ready: work dates, past supervisor contacts, availability, and 2-3 **references** who agreed in advance (teacher, coach, past boss, not family).
- Be honest about availability and dates.
- Use the job title exactly as posted.

After about a week, a short follow-up email to the hiring contact is fine. More than one or two follow-ups is too many.

steps.prompt: An online application has an optional box for a cover letter. You're short on time and applying to five jobs tonight. What's the best approach?

options.text: Write a short tailored letter for the 1-2 jobs you want most, and apply to the rest with tailored resumes.
options.feedback: Smart prioritizing. Quality on your top choices beats copy-paste everywhere.

options.text: Paste the same generic letter into all five.
options.feedback: Generic letters can hurt more than help, especially if you forget to change the company name.

options.text: Skip all five applications until you have a whole free weekend.
options.feedback: Good jobs fill fast. Apply while the posting is fresh.

steps.explain: Spend extra effort where you most want the job, and never send a letter with the wrong company name in it.

steps.prompt: Who makes a good reference? Select all that apply.
options: A former manager who saw your work
A coach or teacher who knows your reliability
Your mom
A volunteer coordinator you worked with
Someone you haven't asked yet
steps.explain: References should have seen you work or lead, and must agree first so they're ready for the call. Family members usually don't count.

steps.prompt: It's fine to send one short, polite follow-up email about a week after applying.
steps.explain: A brief note restating interest shows initiative. Keep it to a few sentences and don't send repeated messages.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Cover letter: why this job, proof with results, thanks.
- Tailor for your top choices; never send a generic letter.
- Complete every field and line up references who said yes.
- One polite follow-up after about a week.

units.title: Interviews and Communication
units.description: Answer interview questions with stories, ask good questions, and communicate like a pro.

levels.title: Interview Prep and STAR Answers
levels.summary: Research, common questions and the STAR method for behavioral questions.

steps.title: Prep beats nerves
steps.body:
Before the interview:
- **Research** the company: what it does, its customers, recent news.
- **Reread the posting** and pick 3 strengths that match it.
- **Prepare stories** for common questions (next step).
- **Plan logistics**: route and parking, or test video and sound for a virtual interview. Arrive 10 minutes early.
- **Dress** one step nicer than people who work there do day to day.

Bring copies of your resume, a pen, and your questions for them.

steps.title: The STAR method
steps.body:
Questions like "Tell me about a time you..." want a real story. Use **STAR**:
- **S**ituation: the background, in a sentence or two
- **T**ask: what you needed to do
- **A**ction: what *you* did (the biggest part)
- **R**esult: what happened, with a number if possible, and what you learned

Aim for about 1-2 minutes per answer. Prepare 4-5 stories you can adapt: a challenge, a mistake, teamwork, leadership, a conflict.

steps.prompt: Put this STAR answer to 'Tell me about a time you handled a problem' in order.
items: At my grocery job, our self-checkout went down during the Saturday rush.
I needed to keep the line moving with just two registers open.
I asked my manager to open a third lane, then walked the line bagging and directing people with few items to the express lane.
Wait times dropped from about 15 minutes to 5, and my manager asked me to train new hires on rush-hour tactics.
steps.explain: Situation, Task, Action, Result. The action is where you show what you personally did; the result proves it worked.

steps.prompt: Match each STAR letter to what it covers.
pairs: The goal or challenge you faced
The outcome and what you learned
steps.explain: Most weak answers skip the Result. Always end with what happened.

steps.prompt: The interviewer asks, 'What's your greatest weakness?' Which answer is best?
options: I'm a perfectionist and work too hard.
I don't really have any weaknesses.
I used to avoid speaking up in groups, so I joined debate club, and now I lead our team's presentations.
I'm usually late, but I'm working on it.
steps.explain: A real, non-critical weakness plus concrete steps to improve shows self-awareness. Cliches and 'none' sound rehearsed, and chronic lateness is a dealbreaker for most jobs.

steps.title: Common questions to prepare
steps.body:
- **Tell me about yourself**: a 60-second summary: what you're doing now, relevant experience, why this job.
- **Why do you want to work here?** Use your research.
- **Tell me about a challenge / mistake / teamwork.** STAR stories.
- **What's your availability?** Be exact and honest.
- **Why should we hire you?** Three strengths matching the posting.

Practice out loud with someone, or record yourself. It feels awkward, and it works.

steps.prompt: Mid-interview you're asked a question you've never thought about and your mind goes blank. What do you do?

options.text: Say 'Good question, let me think for a second,' take a breath, then answer as best you can.
options.feedback: Yes. A short pause looks thoughtful, not weak.

options.text: Make up a story that didn't happen.
options.feedback: Follow-up questions or reference checks can expose it, and it's dishonest.

options.text: Say 'I don't know' and wait for the next question.
options.feedback: Giving up loses the chance to show how you think. Try a partial answer.

steps.explain: Interviewers expect some pauses. Calm thinking out loud beats a rushed or invented answer.

steps.prompt: Write a STAR story about a time you solved a problem or helped a team. Keep each part to one or two sentences.

levels.title: Questions to Ask and Following Up
levels.summary: Smart questions for the interviewer, thank-you notes and handling offers.

steps.title: Interview them back
steps.body:
Near the end you'll hear, "Do you have any questions for us?" Always have 2-3. It shows interest and helps you decide if the job is right.

Good questions:
- "What does a typical day look like in this role?"
- "What does success look like in the first 90 days?"
- "How will I be trained?"
- "What do you like most about working here?"
- "What are the next steps in the process?"

Save pay and benefits questions for later rounds or the offer, unless they bring it up.

steps.prompt: Which are good questions to ask at the end of a first interview? Select all that apply.
options: How will I be trained in the first few weeks?
What does success look like after 3 months?
How soon can I take vacation?
What are the next steps in the hiring process?
What does your company do? (asked without any research)
steps.explain: Questions about training, success and next steps show you're thinking about doing the job well. Asking about time off first, or what the company does, sends the wrong signal.

steps.title: Follow up within a day
steps.body:
Send a short **thank-you email** within 24 hours to each interviewer:
- Thank them for their time.
- Mention one specific thing you discussed.
- Restate your interest in one sentence.

It's three or four sentences, and many applicants skip it.

If they said you'd hear back by a date and that date passes, a polite check-in is fine.

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a thank-you email in order.
items: Subject line: Thank you - Sales Associate interview
Greeting using the interviewer's name
Thanks for their time and one specific detail you enjoyed discussing
One sentence restating your interest and fit
Sign-off with your full name and phone number
steps.explain: Short, specific and fast. A detail from the conversation shows you were listening.

steps.prompt: You get a job offer by phone. The pay is lower than you hoped, and you're waiting to hear from another company. What do you say?

options.text: Thank them, say you're excited, and ask for the offer in writing and a day or two to review it.
options.feedback: Right. It's normal to ask for the details in writing and a short time to decide.

options.text: Accept immediately so they don't change their mind.
options.feedback: Offers rarely vanish because you ask for a day. Accepting on the spot gives up your chance to review or negotiate.

options.text: Say nothing and stop answering their calls while you wait.
options.feedback: Going silent can cost you the offer and burns a bridge.

steps.explain: Get it in writing: pay, schedule, start date, benefits. Then you can compare, negotiate, or contact the other company to say you have an offer.

steps.prompt: If you decide to turn down an offer, it's better to ignore the employer than to tell them.
steps.explain: A short, polite decline keeps the door open. Your paths may cross again.

steps.prompt: When should you send your thank-you email after an interview?
options: Within 24 hours
After one week
Only if you get the job
Never; it's outdated
steps.explain: Within a day keeps you fresh in their mind while they're deciding.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Bring 2-3 questions about the work, training and next steps.
- Send a specific thank-you email within 24 hours.
- Ask for offers in writing and a short time to review.
- Decline politely; never ghost an employer.

levels.title: Email and Phone Etiquette
levels.summary: Professional emails, phone calls and messages that get answered.

steps.title: A professional email
steps.body:
- **Subject**: specific ("Schedule question for Friday shift", not "hey").
- **Greeting**: "Hi Ms. Lopez," or "Hello Sam,".
- **Body**: the point in the first sentence or two. Short paragraphs. One clear ask.
- **Sign-off**: "Thanks," or "Best," plus your full name.

Proofread names and dates. Skip slang, emojis and all caps. Reply within one business day, even if just to say "Got it, I'll have this to you by Thursday."

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a professional email in order.
items: A specific subject line
A greeting with the person's name
Your main point or question in the first sentence
Any needed details, in short paragraphs
A sign-off and your full name
steps.explain: Busy people read the subject and first line. Put what matters there.

steps.prompt: You need to swap a shift. Which message to your manager is best?
options: can u cover me sat
Hi Dana, I have a family event Saturday and can't make my 9-3 shift. Alex agreed to take it and I'd take his Tuesday shift. Does that work for you? Thanks, Jordan
I won't be there Saturday.
Hi Dana! Something came up!!! Lmk
steps.explain: It gives the reason, the exact shift, a solution already arranged, and a clear question. Managers love a problem that arrives with a fix.

steps.title: Phone calls and voicemail
steps.body:
Phone calls still matter for interviews, doctors, landlords and work.

- **Answering**: "Hello, this is Jordan." Take calls from unknown numbers somewhere quiet when you're job hunting.
- **Calling**: state your name and reason in the first sentence. Have notes and something to write with.
- **Voicemail**: name, reason, number (said slowly), best time to reach you, then repeat the number.
- **Your greeting**: set up a simple, professional voicemail message and keep the mailbox from filling up.

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a voicemail to a hiring manager in order.
items: Your name
Why you're calling
Your phone number, said slowly
The best time to reach you
Your number again and a thank-you
steps.explain: Name and reason up front; repeating your number means they don't have to replay the message.

steps.prompt: You're going to be 20 minutes late for your shift because of a flat tire. What do you do?

options.text: Call (or text, if that's the workplace rule) your manager right away, say when you'll arrive, and apologize.
options.feedback: Exactly. Early, clear notice lets them plan around you.

options.text: Just show up 20 minutes late; it's only once.
options.feedback: No-notice lateness looks like you don't care, even if the reason is good.

options.text: Skip the shift since you're late anyway.
options.feedback: A no-call no-show is one of the fastest ways to lose a job.

steps.explain: Communicate before the problem lands on someone else. Learn your workplace's rule for call-outs on day one.

steps.prompt: When sending a work email, it's fine to reply-all to a big group with 'Thanks!'
steps.explain: Reply-all fills everyone's inbox. Reply only to the person who needs it unless the whole group needs your answer.

steps.prompt: Match the situation to the best channel.
pairs: Running late for a shift, right now
Written letter or email, ideally after telling your manager
A sensitive conflict with a coworker
steps.explain: Urgent goes by phone; formal or record-worthy goes in writing; sensitive goes face to face.

steps.prompt: Write a short, professional email asking a teacher or coach to be a reference.

units.title: On the Job
units.description: First-job habits, negotiating pay, and earning side income without tax surprises.

levels.title: First-Job Habits
levels.summary: Reliability, taking feedback, asking good questions and leaving well.

steps.title: Reliability is the first skill
steps.body:
In a first job, being dependable matters more than being brilliant:
- **Show up on time**, every time. On time means ready to work at the start time.
- **Do what you said you'd do**, by when you said.
- **Tell people early** when something will slip.
- **Phone away** unless it's part of the job.
- **Learn names** and treat everyone, from the owner to the cleaning crew, with respect.

Managers give more hours, better shifts, raises and references to people they can count on.

steps.title: Taking feedback and asking questions
steps.body:
**Feedback** is information, not an attack. When you get it:
1. Listen without arguing or making excuses.
2. Ask a clarifying question if needed.
3. Say thanks, and show the change next time.

**Asking questions** is expected when you're new. Make them good ones:
- Try to find the answer first (notes, manual, coworker).
- Batch small questions instead of interrupting every five minutes.
- Write the answer down so you only ask once.

steps.prompt: Your manager tells you, in front of no one, that you've been restocking the wrong way and it's slowing down closing. How do you respond?

options.text: 'Thanks for telling me. Can you show me the right way?' Then do it that way from now on.
options.feedback: Perfect. Calm, curious and quick to improve is exactly what managers want.

options.text: Explain that nobody trained you, so it's not your fault.
options.feedback: Maybe true, but leading with excuses makes feedback harder. Ask to be shown instead.

options.text: Say nothing and keep doing it your way.
options.feedback: Ignoring feedback is a fast way to lose trust and hours.

steps.explain: How you take feedback often matters more than the mistake itself.

steps.prompt: Which habits build trust in a new job? Select all that apply.
options: Arriving a few minutes early, ready to work
Writing down instructions so you only ask once
Scrolling your phone when it's slow
Telling your manager early when you'll miss a deadline
Offering to help coworkers during slow times
steps.explain: Punctuality, note-taking, early warnings and helpfulness all signal that you're reliable. Phone time on the clock does the opposite.

steps.title: Know your basic rights
steps.body:
- You must be paid for **all hours worked**, including required training and opening/closing tasks.
- Most hourly workers get **overtime** (1.5x) for hours over 40 in a week.
- Workers under 18 have **limits on hours and on dangerous tasks** under federal and state child labor laws.
- Keep your own log of hours and compare it with your pay stub.

If something seems wrong, ask HR or your manager first. The U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division takes complaints.

steps.prompt: You've found a better job. Put the steps for leaving your current job well in order.
items: Get the new offer in writing and confirm a start date
Tell your manager in person (or by call) first
Follow up with a short written resignation, giving at least two weeks' notice
Work hard through your last shift and help train your replacement
Thank your manager and coworkers and keep in touch
steps.explain: Never quit before the new offer is solid. Two weeks' notice is the standard courtesy, and a good exit keeps you a reference for years.

steps.prompt: Your employer can require you to do unpaid 'training' before your first paid shift as long as you're new.
steps.explain: Required training for the job generally counts as work time and must be paid for hourly employees. Keep a record and ask about it.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Be on time, do what you said, and warn early about problems.
- Take feedback calmly and show the change.
- Ask good questions and write down the answers.
- Track your hours; you must be paid for all work.
- Leave with two weeks' notice and a good last impression.

levels.title: Negotiating Pay and Raises
levels.summary: Research your market rate, ask with evidence and compare total compensation.

steps.title: Know the numbers
steps.body:
Convert pay so you can compare:

> Hourly x 40 hours x 52 weeks = yearly (full-time)
> Yearly / 2,080 = hourly

Research what the role pays in your area: the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, job postings that list pay (many states now require ranges in postings), and people who do the work.

Also compare **total compensation**: health insurance, 401(k) match, paid time off, schedule, training, and commute.

steps.prompt: A full-time job pays $20 an hour. About what is that per year (40 hours x 52 weeks)?
steps.explain: $20 x 40 = $800 a week. $800 x 52 = **$41,600** a year before taxes.

steps.prompt: A salaried job offers $52,000 a year. What is the equivalent hourly rate for a 2,080-hour work year?
steps.explain: $52,000 / 2,080 = **$25 an hour**. If the job regularly needs 50-hour weeks, the real hourly rate is lower.

steps.title: How to ask
steps.body:
Negotiating is a normal, polite conversation, not a fight.

1. **Be enthusiastic first**: "I'm excited about this role."
2. **Give evidence**: market research, relevant skills, a competing offer.
3. **Make a specific ask**, a bit above your target: "Based on that, I was hoping for $X."
4. **Then stop talking** and listen.

If pay can't move, ask about other things: start date, schedule, a raise review after 6 months, training, extra PTO.

For entry-level hourly jobs there may be little room, but asking politely rarely gets an offer pulled.

steps.prompt: You negotiate a starting salary of $48,000 instead of $45,000. Ignoring future raises, how much more do you earn over 5 years?
steps.explain: $3,000 x 5 = **$15,000**. In reality it's even more, because percentage raises are calculated on the higher base.

steps.prompt: You've worked a year, took on training new hires, and your reviews are strong. You want a raise. What's the best approach?

options.text: Book a meeting with your manager, list your added responsibilities and results, share what the role pays locally, and ask for a specific number.
options.feedback: That's the playbook: evidence, market data, a clear ask, at a planned time.

options.text: Complain to coworkers until word gets to the manager.
options.feedback: Indirect pressure damages trust and rarely gets a raise.

options.text: Threaten to quit without another offer.
options.feedback: If they call your bluff, you're stuck. Only mention leaving if you truly would.

steps.explain: Raises go to people who make their value easy to see. Keep a running list of wins all year so the evidence is ready.

steps.prompt: You earn $40,000 and get a 3% raise. What is your new salary?
steps.explain: $40,000 x 0.03 = $1,200. New salary **$41,200**. If prices rose about 3% that year, your buying power stayed about flat.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Your regular salary or hourly rate
Pay plus benefits like insurance and retirement match
Paid time off for vacation or sick days
The lowest to highest pay an employer plans for a role
steps.explain: A slightly lower salary with great insurance and a 401(k) match can be worth more than a higher salary with none.

steps.prompt: Pick a job you might want. Look up its typical pay in your area, then write the exact sentence you'd use to ask for more.
steps.placeholder: Job: ___. Typical pay: ___. My ask: 'I'm excited about this role. Based on ___, I was hoping for ___.'

levels.title: Side Income and Freelancing
levels.summary: Pricing your work, self-employment tax and setting money aside.

steps.title: Side hustles are small businesses
steps.body:
Tutoring, lawn care, dog walking, editing videos, reselling, delivery apps: these make you **self-employed** (an independent contractor).

That means:
- **No one withholds tax** from what you earn.
- You can deduct legitimate **business expenses** (supplies, some mileage, a portion of software).
- You might receive a **1099** form, but **all income is taxable** whether or not a form arrives.
- You need to **track** income and expenses yourself: a simple spreadsheet works.

steps.prompt: You tutor 3 students, each for 2 hours a week, at $25 an hour. How much do you earn in a 4-week month?
steps.explain: 3 x 2 = 6 hours a week. 6 x $25 = $150 a week. $150 x 4 = **$600** a month.

steps.title: Self-employment tax
steps.body:
As an employee, you pay 7.65% FICA and your employer pays 7.65%. Self-employed, you pay **both halves: 15.3%** in **self-employment tax** (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare), on top of regular income tax.

- It applies once net self-employment earnings reach **$400** in a year.
- It's figured on 92.35% of your net profit (a built-in adjustment), and you can deduct half of it for income tax.
- If you'll owe $1,000 or more, the IRS expects **quarterly estimated payments**.

> A simple habit: move 25-30% of every side-gig payment into a separate savings account for taxes.

steps.prompt: You earned $8,000 freelancing this year and set aside 25% for taxes. How much did you set aside?
steps.explain: $8,000 x 0.25 = **$2,000**. Your actual bill depends on expenses, other income and deductions, but this buffer prevents an April shock.

steps.prompt: Your net self-employment profit is $10,000. Self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net profit. What is your self-employment tax? Round to the nearest dollar.

steps.title: Price your work
steps.body:
Beginners often charge too little. To set a rate:
- Check what others nearby charge for similar work.
- Count unpaid time: travel, messaging, prep, invoicing.
- Remember taxes and costs come out of what you charge.

Raise prices for new clients once you're booked up. Get the important details in writing, even a text: what you'll do, price, and when you'll be paid.

Platforms (delivery, freelance marketplaces) take a cut. Compare your earnings **after** their fees, gas and wear on your car.

steps.prompt: You drive for a delivery app and made $4,800 this year. You didn't get a 1099 form. What should you do at tax time?

options.text: Report the $4,800 as self-employment income, subtract business expenses like mileage, and pay what you owe.
options.feedback: Correct. All income is taxable whether or not a form arrives, and tracking mileage can lower your bill.

options.text: Skip it: no form means the IRS doesn't know.
options.feedback: Platforms often report payments anyway. Unreported income can lead to back taxes, penalties and interest.

options.text: Report it as a gift from a friend.
options.feedback: That's tax fraud. It's business income.

steps.explain: Keep a mileage log and receipts from day one. Business deductions are only as good as your records.

steps.prompt: Which are good habits for side income? Select all that apply.
options: Keep a spreadsheet of income and expenses
Move part of each payment into a tax savings account
Mix all business and personal spending in one pile
Track mileage for business driving
Get the price and scope in writing before starting
steps.explain: Clean records and a tax buffer make tax season easy. Mixing everything together makes it hard to prove deductions.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Side income is self-employment: no withholding.
- Self-employment tax is 15.3% once you net $400+, plus income tax.
- Set aside 25-30% of every payment.
- Track income, expenses and mileage.
- All income is taxable, form or no form.

units.title: Planning Your Career
units.description: Build skills that compound and compare paths by cost, time and return.

levels.title: Skills That Compound
levels.summary: The skills that pay off in every job, and how to keep building them.

steps.title: Some skills transfer everywhere
steps.body:
Job titles change; some skills pay off in every one:
- **Clear writing and speaking**
- **Reliability**: doing what you said
- **Problem solving**: figuring things out without step-by-step instructions
- **Working with people**: teamwork, handling conflict, customer service
- **Learning fast**: picking up new tools and systems
- **Numbers and money**: estimates, spreadsheets, budgets

These **compound**: each job builds on them, and people who have them get trusted with more, which teaches them more.

steps.prompt: Match each transferable skill to an example of using it.
pairs: Explaining a problem clearly to a manager by email
Figuring out why the inventory count doesn't match
Covering a coworker's task during a rush
Teaching yourself a new scheduling app in a day
steps.explain: When you describe experience in resumes and interviews, name these skills and give an example.

steps.title: Build skills on purpose
steps.body:
- **Say yes to stretch tasks** at work: training others, handling a tough customer, learning a new system.
- **Learn tools** employers ask for: spreadsheets, a trade tool, a coding language, a design app.
- **Earn credentials** that matter in your field: a CPR card, a forklift certification, an industry certificate.
- **Keep a brag file**: a running list of wins, numbers and praise. It feeds your resume, interviews and raise requests.
- **Find mentors**: people a few steps ahead who'll answer questions.

steps.prompt: Your manager asks if anyone wants to learn the store's ordering system. It's extra work with no extra pay right now. What do you do?

options.text: Volunteer. It's a new skill, shows initiative, and is the kind of experience that leads to a promotion or a stronger resume.
options.feedback: Good long-term thinking. Skills and trust compound into better roles and pay.

options.text: Decline: never do anything you're not paid extra for.
options.feedback: Sometimes reasonable, but turning down every growth chance slows your career.

options.text: Volunteer, then avoid actually learning it.
options.feedback: That damages trust more than saying no would have.

steps.explain: Stretch tasks are how you get experience you can't get from a job description. If it grows into a lot of extra work, that's a good basis for a raise conversation.

steps.prompt: Which belong in a 'brag file'? Select all that apply.
options: A thank-you email from a customer
The number of new hires you trained
A record of a project you finished early
Gossip about coworkers
A certification you earned
steps.explain: Praise, numbers, finished projects and credentials are evidence for resumes and raises. Gossip isn't.

steps.prompt: Once you've finished school, learning new skills mostly stops mattering for your career.
steps.explain: Tools and industries keep changing. People who keep learning, on the job or through courses and certificates, tend to keep moving up.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of learning a new job skill on purpose in order.
items: Pick one skill that shows up in jobs you want
Find a way to learn it (course, mentor, practice project)
Practice it on a real task at work or in a project
Record the result in your brag file
Add it to your resume with a result
steps.explain: Learning plus a real use plus a recorded result gives you something to show employers.

steps.prompt: Start your brag file now. Write three things you've done that you're proud of, with a number if you can.

levels.title: College, Trades or Certificates?
levels.summary: Compare paths by total cost, time, earnings and fit.

steps.title: Many paths work
steps.body:
- **Four-year college**: needed for many professional careers (engineering, teaching, nursing BSN, accounting). Highest cost and time.
- **Community college**: two-year degrees and transfer paths at a much lower cost.
- **Apprenticeship**: learn a trade (electrician, plumber, HVAC) on the job while **earning a paycheck**, plus classes.
- **Certificates**: short programs (weeks to a year) in areas like IT support, welding, medical assisting or CDL truck driving.
- **Military**: training plus education benefits.

The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook shows each job's typical training, pay and growth.

steps.title: Think like an investor: ROI
steps.body:
**Return on investment (ROI)** compares what a path costs with how much more you'll earn.

Count the full cost:
- Tuition, fees, books, tools
- Interest on any loans
- **Lost wages** while you're in school full-time

Then estimate the earnings boost and how long it takes to pay back:

> Payback years = total cost / yearly earnings increase

Also weigh things money can't measure: what you'd enjoy, job demand where you want to live, and the physical demands of the work.

steps.prompt: A 6-month IT support certificate costs $4,000. It raises your pay from $32,000 to $40,000 a year. How many years until the raise pays back the cost?
steps.explain: The raise is $8,000 a year. $4,000 / $8,000 = **0.5 years**, about 6 months. That's a strong ROI, if the jobs exist where you live.

steps.prompt: A degree costs $40,000 in total and you expect it to raise your pay by $10,000 a year. How many years to pay back the cost (ignoring interest and lost wages)?
steps.explain: $40,000 / $10,000 = **4 years**. Counting loan interest and wages you gave up while in school, the real payback is longer.

steps.prompt: You like hands-on work, want to avoid debt, and want to earn as soon as possible. Which path fits best to explore first?

options.text: A registered apprenticeship in a trade like electrician or HVAC, where you earn while you learn.
options.feedback: Strong fit. Apprentices are paid from the start and finish with a credential and little or no debt.

options.text: An expensive private four-year degree in a field you're not interested in.
options.feedback: High cost and a poor fit for hands-on goals and avoiding debt.

options.text: Wait a few years and decide later.
options.feedback: Waiting is okay if you're working and exploring, but doing nothing on purpose delays every option.

steps.explain: Match the path to your interests, money situation and timeline. You can also stack paths: a trade now, a degree later, often with employer help.

steps.prompt: Match each path to its key feature.
pairs: Low-cost two-year degrees and transfer paths
Short, focused training for one job type
steps.explain: There's no single right path. The right one fits the job you want and the cost you can handle.

steps.prompt: Which should you count in the full cost of a full-time program? Select all that apply.
options: Tuition and fees
Books, tools and supplies
Wages you give up while studying
Interest on student loans
What your friends think of the school
steps.explain: Tuition, materials, lost wages and interest are all real costs. Opinions matter for fit, but not for the price tag.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- College, community college, apprenticeships, certificates and the military can all lead to good careers.
- Count full cost, including lost wages and interest.
- Payback years = total cost / yearly earnings increase.
- Check real job demand and pay in the BLS handbook.
- Fit matters: pick work you can see yourself doing for years.

steps.prompt: Pick two paths that interest you. For each, write the total cost, time to finish, and expected pay from the BLS handbook. Which has the better payback?
steps.placeholder: Path 1: cost ___, time ___, pay ___. Path 2: cost ___, time ___, pay ___.

levels.title: Your Career Game Plan
levels.summary: Set a direction, test it cheaply, and review it every year.

steps.title: Test before you commit
steps.body:
You don't have to know your whole career at 18. You do want to make good bets.

Cheap ways to test a field before spending years on it:
- **Informational interviews**: 20-minute chats with people who do the work. Ask what they like, what's hard, and how they got there.
- **Job shadowing** for a day
- **Part-time or summer jobs** near the field
- **Short online courses** or a small project

Each test either builds excitement or saves you from an expensive wrong turn.

steps.prompt: Which are good questions for an informational interview? Select all that apply.
options: What does a normal week look like for you?
What do you wish you'd known when you started?
Can you get me a job at your company?
Which skills or training matter most to get hired?
How much money do you have in savings?
steps.explain: Ask about the work, lessons learned and how to break in. Don't ask for a job directly or about their personal finances. If it goes well, they'll often offer to help.

steps.title: Goals with a timeline
steps.body:
Turn a direction into steps. A simple plan:
- **1-year goal**: a specific job, certification or skill
- **3 next actions** that move you toward it this month
- **Check-in date** every few months

Make goals specific: not "get better with computers" but "earn the IT support certificate by June."

Plans change, and that's fine. Reviewing your plan once a year keeps you choosing your direction instead of drifting.

steps.prompt: Which goal is written most usefully?
options: Be successful
Get into healthcare someday
Finish the CNA certification course and apply to three nursing homes by August 1
Make a lot of money
steps.explain: It's specific, measurable and has a deadline, so you know exactly what to do next and when you've done it.

steps.prompt: Put a career-planning cycle in order.
items: List interests and jobs you'd like to explore
Test them cheaply with conversations, shadowing or short courses
Choose a direction and set a specific 1-year goal
Take monthly actions toward the goal
Review and adjust the plan every year
steps.explain: Explore, test, commit, act, review. Then repeat as you learn more about what you like.

steps.prompt: Six months into a certificate program, you realize you dislike the work. What's the best move?

options.text: Talk to people in the field and an advisor, consider whether finishing still opens useful doors, and use what you learned to choose a better-fitting next step.
options.feedback: Thoughtful. Sometimes finishing is worth it; sometimes switching is. Information makes the call.

options.text: Push through no matter what, because quitting is failure.
options.feedback: Sunk costs shouldn't trap you in a career you'll dislike for decades.

options.text: Drop out today without a plan.
options.feedback: Leaving might be right, but have a next step before you stop.

steps.explain: Changing course is normal. Decide based on future value, not on what you've already spent.

steps.prompt: Most people need to have their entire career figured out by 18.
steps.explain: Most people change jobs and even fields several times. What matters is building skills and making informed next steps.

steps.prompt: Write your 1-year career goal, three actions for this month, and your next check-in date.
